tasks.description: Use `@dataclass` to create a `Point` class with `x: float` and `y: float`. Create a point and print it.
tasks.hint:
`from dataclasses import dataclass`
`@dataclass class Point: x: float; y: float`
Dataclasses automatically generate `__init__`, `__repr__`, and `__eq__` for you!
Create: `p = Point(1.0, 2.0)` — no `__init__` needed.
tasks.solution:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float

p = Point(1.0, 2.0)
print(p)
tasks.walkthrough:
The decorator reads the two annotated fields and writes `__init__` and `__repr__` for you.
Printing shows the class name and every field, which the generated `__repr__` provides.

tasks.description: Add a default value to a dataclass field: `name: str = 'Unknown'`. Show that creating an instance without name uses the default.
tasks.hint:
Fields with defaults: `name: str = 'Unknown'`
Fields WITH defaults must come AFTER fields WITHOUT defaults (same rule as function params).
`Person()` uses 'Unknown'; `Person('Alice')` uses 'Alice'.
tasks.solution:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Person:
    age: int
    name: str = 'Unknown'

print(Person(30))
print(Person(25, 'Alice'))
tasks.walkthrough:
`name` has a default, so it comes after `age`, which doesn't.
Creating a Person with just an age fills in 'Unknown'; supplying a name overrides it.

tasks.description: Use `field(default_factory=list)` to give a dataclass an empty list attribute that's unique per instance.
tasks.hint:
`from dataclasses import dataclass, field`
NEVER use `tags: list = []` as a default — all instances share the same list!
Correct: `tags: list = field(default_factory=list)` — creates a new list per instance.
tasks.solution:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Article:
    title: str
    tags: list = field(default_factory=list)

a = Article('First')
b = Article('Second')
a.tags.append('python')

print(a.tags)
print(b.tags)
tasks.walkthrough:
`default_factory=list` means each new Article gets its own empty list.
Appending to one doesn't affect the other, which is the whole point. With `tags: list = []` both would show ['python'].

tasks.description: Create a frozen dataclass `Color` with r, g, b fields. Show that trying to modify a field raises an error.
tasks.hint:
`@dataclass(frozen=True)` makes instances immutable — like a named tuple.
Trying to set an attribute: `color.r = 255` raises `FrozenInstanceError`.
Frozen dataclasses are hashable and can be used as dict keys or in sets.
tasks.walkthrough:
`frozen=True` makes the generated class reject attribute assignment after creation.
The attempt raises FrozenInstanceError, which is caught and reported instead of crashing.

tasks.description: Add a `__post_init__` method to validate that a `Rectangle` dataclass has positive width and height.
tasks.hint:
`__post_init__(self)` is called automatically after `__init__` by the dataclass machinery.
Inside it, add validation: `if self.width <= 0: raise ValueError('Width must be positive')`
This is cleaner than overriding `__init__` entirely.
tasks.walkthrough:
The generated `__init__` sets the fields and then calls `__post_init__`, where the checks live.
A valid rectangle is created normally; a negative width raises ValueError before the object is usable.

lesson.intro:
A lot of classes exist just to hold a few fields. Writing `__init__`, `__repr__`
and `__eq__` for every one is tedious. `@dataclass` generates them from a list
of fields with type hints. Less code, fewer mistakes.

sections.heading: The basics
sections.body:
Decorate the class and list the fields with type hints. You get a
constructor that takes them in order, a readable `repr`, and equality
that compares field by field.
sections.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float

p = Point(1.0, 2.0)
print(p)
print(p.x)
print(p == Point(1.0, 2.0))

sections.heading: Defaults
sections.body:
Give a field a default with `=`. Fields with defaults must come after
fields without, the same rule as function parameters.
sections.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Person:
    name: str = 'Unknown'
    age: int = 0

print(Person())
print(Person('Alice', 30))

sections.heading: Mutable defaults need default_factory
sections.body:
`tags: list = []` would share one list between every instance, which is
almost never what you want. `field(default_factory=list)` calls `list()`
fresh for each new object.
sections.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Article:
    title: str
    tags: list = field(default_factory=list)

a = Article('One')
b = Article('Two')
a.tags.append('python')
print(a.tags, b.tags)

sections.heading: frozen: read-only objects
sections.body:
`@dataclass(frozen=True)` makes instances immutable. Trying to assign a
field raises FrozenInstanceError. Frozen dataclasses can be used as
dictionary keys and set members.
sections.output:
Cannot change a frozen dataclass
{Color(r=255, g=0, b=0): 'red'}

sections.heading: __post_init__: validation
sections.body:
The generated `__init__` stores the fields, then calls `__post_init__` if
you define one. That's the spot for checks.
sections.output:
Rectangle(width=2, height=3)
Width and height must be positive

watch_out: Forgetting the type hint. `x = 0` in a dataclass body is a class variable, not a field; it must be `x: int = 0`.
Using `[]` or `{}` as a default. Use `field(default_factory=list)` or `dict`.
Frozen dataclasses can't be changed even inside their own methods.
`@dataclass` needs the brackets only when passing options like `frozen=True`.
